title: "1. Setting up models"
---

```{r, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      fig.retina = 2, message = FALSE)
project <- normalizePath("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018")
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = project)
fitted <- file.exists(file.path(project, "results", "fits.rds"))
knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018/model.R")
```

A model in dMod2 is a chain of function objects. Each maps its input to its output and returns,
together with the output, the derivatives of the output with respect to the parameters:

| class | constructors | mapping |
|---|---|---|
| `parfn` | `P()`, `Pexpl()`, `Pimpl()` | parameter transformation: outer parameters to the inner parameters of every condition, or parameters to the steady state of a network (`Pimpl()`) |
| `prdfn` | `Xs()`, `Xf()` | parameters to the trajectories of the states, the solution of the ODE, with their sensitivities (`Xs()`) or without (`Xf()`) |
| `obsfn` | `Y()` | states to observables, and observables to their standard deviations, the error model |
| `objfn` | `normL2()`, `constraintL2()`, `datapointL2()` | parameters to the objective $-2 \log L$, its gradient and its Hessian |

In the guide, `p` and `pSS` are `parfn`s, `x` is the `prdfn`, `g` the observables and `e` the
error model, both `obsfn`s, and `obj` the `objfn`.

`*` concatenates two function objects by the chain rule: for $y = g(x(p(\theta)))$ it returns $y$
together with

$$\frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta} = \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial p}\,
\frac{\partial p}{\partial \theta},$$

each factor computed exactly by the object it belongs to, the middle one from the sensitivity
equations of the ODE. `g*x*pSS*p` is again a `prdfn`, from the outer parameters to the
observables of all conditions. `normL2(data, g*x*pSS*p, e)` is the `objfn` an optimiser
minimises, and `+` adds `objfn`s, for example a prior.

The product of two `parfn`s is a `parfn`. `pSS*p` first takes the outer parameters to the inner
parameters of each condition and then those to the steady state. A transformation is built in such
stages wherever one step depends on the result of another: a reparametrisation, the values per
condition, an equilibration.

The inner parameters are the symbols of the equations: rate constants, initial values, volumes,
scales, offsets and standard deviations. Every condition has its own values of them. The outer
parameters are the parameters of the fit. The `parfn` computes the inner parameters of every
condition from the outer ones, and an outer parameter that enters several conditions is one
parameter for all of them.

The guide builds and analyses the model of Oppelt et al. (2018, npj Syst Biol Appl 4:23): NFκB
signalling in HepG2 cells stimulated with TNFα. The code is the project
[`examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018`](https://github.com/dModverse/dMod2/tree/master/examples/oppeltNPJSystBiolAppl2018);
each chapter shows a part of its scripts. This chapter goes through `model.R`, from the reactions
to the `objfn`. The model is the full model of the publication, before any reduction:
[chapter 2](guide-symmetries.html) removes its symmetries, [chapter 5](guide-profiles.html) the
parts the data do not determine.

```{r setup}
```

## Reactions

In unstimulated cells NFκB is held in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor IκBα. TNFα activates its
receptor, and the active receptor activates the kinase IKK. IKK phosphorylates IκBα and NFκB in
their complex; phosphorylated IκBα is released and degraded. Free NFκB enters the nucleus and
induces the transcription of IκBα and of A20. New IκBα enters the nucleus, binds NFκB and exports
it; A20 inhibits the activation of IKK. Both negative feedbacks make nuclear NFκB oscillate in
damped waves. IKK passes through four states: inactive (`Ikk`), active (`pIkk`), doubly
phosphorylated (`ppIkk`) and refractory (`iIkk`), from which it recovers.

`addReaction()` adds a reaction with its educts, products and rate to an `eqnlist`. The model has
two compartments: the cytoplasm, the default compartment of volume 1, and the nucleus, of volume
`Vnuc` relative to it. `assignCompartment()` places the four nuclear species there. A rate is a
concentration rate in the compartment of its educts. Reaction $r$ with rate $v_r$ in a frame of
volume $V_{f(r)}$ moves the amount $V_{f(r)} v_r$ per unit time, and a species $i$ in a compartment
of volume $V_i$ changes its concentration by that amount divided by $V_i$:

$$\dot x_i = \frac{1}{V_i} \sum_r S_{ri}\, V_{f(r)}\, v_r(x, p),$$

with $S_{ri}$ the stoichiometric coefficient of species $i$ in reaction $r$. A reaction within one
compartment contributes $S_{ri} v_r$; the import of free NFκB into the nucleus contributes
$v_r / V_\mathrm{nuc}$ to nuclear NFκB, and the export of the nuclear complex $V_\mathrm{nuc} v_r$ to
the cytoplasmic complex.

TNFα in the medium is not used up by the cells. The reaction `TNF -> TNF + TNFR` writes it as a
catalyst: TNFα appears on both sides, so its concentration stays constant, while it produces active
receptors. As a state of its own, TNFα can be set by an event at the time of the stimulus (section
[Events](#events)).

The model of the guide extends the publication at the receptor in two ways, which
[chapter 2](guide-symmetries.html) and [chapter 5](guide-profiles.html) take out again. The
receptors saturate, with the constant `K_R`, and besides TNFα a ligand `Lig` activates them, which
the cells secrete at the rate `prod_L` and which decays with `degrad_L`; no measurement sees it.
The receptors are activated at the rate

$$v = \frac{\mathrm{uptake}\,(\mathrm{TNF} + \mathrm{Lig})}{1 + K_R\,(\mathrm{TNF} + \mathrm{Lig})},$$

which for `K_R = 0` and without the ligand is the rate `uptake * TNF` of the publication.

```{r reactions}
```

```{r}
length(reactions$states)
length(reactions$rates)
as.eqnvec(reactions)[c("NfkIkb", "nNfk", "TNF", "TNFR", "Lig")]
```

The equation of `NfkIkb` has the export of the nuclear complex with the factor `Vnuc`, that of
`nNfk` the import with `1/Vnuc`; `TNF` has the right-hand side 0.

Several reactions share their rate constants through factors named `eta_`: the phosphorylation of
IκBα by `ppIkk` runs at `eta_s_ppIkk` times the rate by `pIkk`, the formation of the nuclear
complex at `eta_form_complex_nuc` times that in the cytoplasm. A factor of 1 states that the two
processes are equally fast; the prior of section [Objective](#objective) is centred there.

## Observables

The data are live-cell imaging of NFκB and A20 fused to GFP, quantitative immunoblots of the
cytoplasm, and immunoblots after immunoprecipitation (IP) of NFκB or IκBα, which measure the
proteins bound to the precipitated one. An imaging signal or a blot measures the sum of the species
that have the epitope, up to a scale `s_` and an offset `off_`. The fluorescence of the imaging
readouts bleaches exponentially with the rate `tau_`. The data are on the natural log scale, and so
are the observables:

$$y = \log\bigl((s\, x + o)\, e^{-\tau t}\bigr) = \log(s\, x + o) - \tau t.$$

On the log scale an error of constant size is a relative error of the signal. The helper `logOf()`
writes the expressions; the last observable, the ratio of cytoplasmic NFκB to IκBα, is a ratio of
two sums of species and needs no scale.

```{r observables}
```

## Error model

The blots come with a standard deviation per point, in the column `sigma` of the data. The imaging
readouts have none; the error model gives them a standard deviation of their own on the log scale,
estimated with the other parameters. Rows with a value in `sigma` do not use the error model.

```{r errors}
```

## Steady state

The cells rest before TNFα is added. Their state at the time of the stimulus is a steady state of
the network without TNFα, $f(x, p) = 0$. These equations do not determine $x$ alone: the reactions
move NFκB and IKK between their forms but neither produce nor degrade them, and the totals are
conserved. A conserved quantity is a vector $w$ in the null space of the stoichiometric matrix,
$S w = 0$; it conserves the amount $\sum_i w_i V_i x_i$, which `conservedQuantities()` writes on the
concentrations with the volumes of their compartments:

```{r}
conservedQuantities(reactions)
```

NFκB in the nucleus enters its total with the factor `Vnuc`, since the total is an amount. `TNF`
is conserved because no reaction changes it; a conserved quantity of a single species has the
name of that species.

`Pimpl()` builds a `parfn` that solves the steady state numerically in every evaluation. It stacks
the right-hand side and the conservation laws $C(p)\,x = T$, with the totals $T$ as parameters
(`totalNfk`, `totalIkk`), into

$$G(x, p) = \begin{pmatrix} f(x, p) \\ C(p)\, x - T \end{pmatrix} = 0,$$

and solves it by pseudo-transient continuation: implicit Euler steps of $\dot x = f(x, p)$ on the
manifold of the conservation laws, with a pseudo-time step that grows as the residual falls: the
iteration follows the flow far from the root and becomes Newton's method near it, and so reaches a
stable steady state, the one the cells rest in. A state that no reaction changes, `TNF`, is held at
its given value, here 0, and the ligand rests at `prod_L / degrad_L`, so that the receptors are
active at rest as well. The derivatives of the root follow from the implicit function theorem:
$G(x(p), p) = 0$ for all $p$ gives

$$\frac{\partial G}{\partial x}\, \frac{\partial x}{\partial p} = -\frac{\partial G}{\partial p},$$

a linear system with the Jacobian of the stacked equations, which is regular where the steady
state is isolated within its conservation class. A root depends on the parameters only, never on
the calls before it, so the `objfn` is the same function of its parameters in every call.

```{r steadystate}
```

`steadyStates()` is the symbolic alternative: it solves the balance equations in closed form where
the solution is a ratio of positive sums, and the solution enters `P()` like any other assignment.
For this network, with basal phosphorylation and transcription feeding back on each other, it finds
no such form, and the guide uses `Pimpl()`.

## Events

An event changes a state at a time, or when a root condition crosses zero. Its time and its value
can be parameters, and the sensitivities pass it: an event that replaces $x_k$ by $v(p)$ at time
$t_e$ sets $\partial x_k / \partial p = \partial v / \partial p$ there and leaves the other rows
unchanged. Here an event adds TNFα at time 0: the system starts from the steady state of `pSS`,
computed at `TNF = 0`, and the event replaces `TNF` by `dose_TNF`. The dose is the unit of TNFα,
1 in the stimulated condition and 0 in the control.

## ODE model

`odemodel()` generates C++ code for the right-hand side and for the sensitivity equations, the
derivatives of the states with respect to every parameter and initial value. `Xs()` turns it into
the `prdfn` `x` and sets the options of the solver. `Y(observables, x)` builds the `obsfn` `g` on
the states of `x`, and `Y(errors, g)` the `obsfn` `e` on the observables of `g`. `compile = FALSE`
defers the compilation, so that all parts are compiled together in the section
[Compile](#compile).

```{r odemodel}
```

The default backend `"cppDE"` integrates with a BDF method and computes first-order and, with
`deriv2 = TRUE`, second-order sensitivities. `backend = "Sundials"` uses CVODES, `backend =
"deSolve"` the solvers of deSolve.

At every step the solver estimates the local error of each state $x_i$ and accepts the step if

$$|\varepsilon_i| \le \mathrm{atol} + \mathrm{rtol}\,|x_i| .$$

| option | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `atol` | `1e-6` | absolute error per step, in the units of the states |
| `rtol` | `1e-6` | relative error per step |
| `maxsteps` | `1e6` | steps of one solve before it fails |
| `maxattempts` | `50` | rejected steps in a row before the solve fails |
| `hini` | `0` | first step, 0 estimates it |
| `sensErrCon` | `TRUE` | (`optionsSens` only) whether the sensitivities enter the error test |

`atol` has to be small against the states that matter: a state around $10^{-3}$ keeps three correct
digits under `atol = 1e-6`. The totals of NFκB and IKK are of order 1, and the observables are
logarithms, which magnify the relative error of a small state; `model.R` sets `rtol = 1e-8` and
`atol = 1e-10`. The error of the solver is noise in $-2 \log L$ and its gradient; the section
[Solver error](#solver-error) measures it.

## Data

The data of the publication are a CSV file with 15 lines of header. Each row names the readout, the
time in minutes, the value, its standard deviation, the treatment, the compound, the cell type and
the blot scale. `model.R` renames the readouts to the names of the observables and keeps HepG2
cells without a compound: 312 points in two conditions, untreated and stimulated with TNFα.

```{r data}
```

```{r}
table(hepg2$name, hepg2$condition)
```

`as.datalist()` splits the data into a `datalist`, one data frame per condition; `keepCovariates`
keeps the columns that describe a condition. `covariates()` returns them as a table with one row
per condition:

```{r}
covariates(data)
```

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}
plotData(data, name %in% c("nucNFkB", "cytNFkB", "A20GFP", "IkBa", "pIkBa", "pIKK")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "time [min]", y = "log signal [a.u.]")
```

Nuclear NFκB rises within 25 minutes of TNFα, falls, and returns in a second, smaller wave at about
two hours; cytoplasmic NFκB moves the opposite way. IκBα falls while NFκB enters the nucleus, and
A20 rises with a delay.

## Transformation

The `parfn` `p` states how every inner parameter follows from the outer ones. `define()` and
`insert()` build it as assignments:

- `define("x <- x", x = ...)` starts with every parameter of `pSS`, `x`, `g` and `e` as itself,
  except the states, whose values come from the steady state.
- `insert("x <- exp(x)", x = .currentSymbols)` puts every symbol on the natural log scale. The data
  determine the order of magnitude of a rate constant, and the log keeps it positive.
- `define("TNF <- 0")` sets TNFα to 0 for the steady state.
- `branch(covariates(data))` copies the assignments once per condition, and `define(...,
  conditionMatch = )` sets the dose in each.

`P()` turns the assignments into the `parfn`.

```{r transformation}
```

```{r}
p
```

## Inner and outer parameters

```{r}
length(getParameters(pSS, x, g, e))
getEquations(p, conditions = "TNF")[c("dose_TNF", "TNF", "totalNfk", "Vnuc")]
getEquations(p, conditions = "control")[c("dose_TNF", "TNF")]
```

The inner parameters include the 23 initial values; the steady state replaces them. The dose is a
number per condition, every other inner parameter the exponential of one outer parameter shared by
both conditions.

## Compile

`compile()` compiles all generated sources into one shared object in `getOption("dMod2.outdir")`,
here `build/` in the project. The object files are reused while the generated code and the
compiler flags do not change.

```{r compile}
```

```{r}
length(getParameters(prd))
```

The `prdfn` `prd = g*x*pSS*p` maps the `r length(getParameters(prd))` outer parameters to the
observables of the two conditions.

## Objective

`normL2(data, prd, e)` returns an `objfn`. With the predictions $f_j(\theta)$ of the data points
$y_j$ and their standard deviations $\sigma_j$, from the data or from the error model, it computes

$$-2 \log L(\theta) = \sum_j \left( \frac{(y_j - f_j(\theta))^2}{\sigma_j(\theta)^2} +
\log \sigma_j(\theta)^2 \right) + \text{const},$$

with its gradient and the Gauss-Newton approximation of its Hessian, both from the sensitivities.
The term $\log \sigma_j^2$ is the normalisation of the Gaussian density; it keeps the estimated
standard deviations of the imaging readouts from growing without bound.

Every parameter gets a weak Gaussian prior on the log scale,

$$-2 \log \pi(\theta) = \sum_k \left( \frac{\theta_k - \mu_k}{s_k} \right)^2,$$

with mean $\mu_k = -1$ and standard deviation $s_k = 4$: one standard deviation is a factor of
$e^4 \approx 55$. The offsets have mean $-2$ and standard deviation 2, since a background lies below
the signal, and the factors `eta_` mean 0, a factor of 1. The prior is far wider than what the data
determine where they determine a parameter; where they do not, it keeps the parameter at a finite
value. The objective is then $-2 \log$ of the posterior up to a constant, and its minimum exists
without bounds on the parameters. `constraintL2()` builds the prior as another `objfn`, and `+`
adds it to the data term.

```{r objective}
```

## Evaluation

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !fitted}
cat("> Results pending: `results/fits.rds` of the project is written by `fit.R`.\n")
```

An `objfn` called with outer parameters returns the value, the gradient and the Hessian. At the
best fit of [chapter 4](guide-optimization.html), with the parameters that [chapter 2](guide-symmetries.html)
fixes, `gauge`:

```{r gauge, echo = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = fitted}
best <- as.parvec(readRDS("results/fits.rds"))
value <- obj(best, fixed = gauge)
value$value
c(data = attr(value, "data"), prior = attr(value, "prior"))
max(abs(value$gradient))
dim(value$hessian)
```

The value has two parts, kept as attributes: the data term and the prior. At the optimum the
gradient is close to zero.

The prediction at these parameters against the data. With `errfn = e`, `plotCombined()` draws one
standard deviation of the error model as a band around the prediction of the imaging readouts:

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7, eval = fitted}
times <- seq(0, 360, length.out = 361)
plotCombined(prd(times, c(best, gauge), deriv = FALSE), data, errfn = e) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y", ncol = 4) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "time [min]", y = "log signal [a.u.]")
```

## Solver error

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !fitted}
cat("> Results pending: `results/fits.rds` of the project is written by `fit.R`.\n")
```

The solver solves each step to its tolerances, so the value and the gradient of the `objfn` have
an error that changes with the parameters like noise. The `objfn` is built again with tolerances
three orders of magnitude tighter, and the difference to it is the error of the settings of
`model.R`:

```{r, eval = fitted}
tight <- normL2(data, g * Xs(model, options = list(atol = 1e-13, rtol = 1e-11)) * pSS * p, e) +
  constraintL2(mu, sigma = sigma)
reference <- tight(best, fixed = gauge)
c(value = value$value - reference$value,
  gradient = max(abs(value$gradient - reference$gradient[names(value$gradient)])))
```

The error over a range of tolerances, `atol` two orders below `rtol`:

```{r, fig.height = 3, eval = fitted}
scan <- do.call(rbind, lapply(4:9, function(k) {
  xk <- Xs(model, options = list(atol = 10^-(k + 2), rtol = 10^-k))
  vk <- (normL2(data, g * xk * pSS * p, e) + constraintL2(mu, sigma = sigma))(best, fixed = gauge)
  data.frame(rtol  = 10^-k,
             name  = c("value", "gradient"),
             error = c(abs(vk$value - reference$value),
                       max(abs(vk$gradient - reference$gradient[names(vk$gradient)]))))
}))
scan$name <- factor(scan$name, c("value", "gradient"))
ggplot2::ggplot(scan, ggplot2::aes(rtol, error, color = name)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() +
  ggplot2::geom_point() +
  ggplot2::scale_x_log10(breaks = 10^-(4:9), labels = scales::label_log()) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10(breaks = scales::breaks_log(8), labels = scales::label_log()) +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "error against rtol = 1e-11", color = NULL) +
  scale_color_dMod() +
  theme_dMod()
```

The error falls about in proportion to `rtol`. It sets what the optimiser can resolve. `trust()`
stops when the change of the objective, its predicted change or its largest gradient entry falls
below `ftol`, `mtol` or `gtol`, by default `1e-6` each. A tolerance below the noise of the
objective cannot be met reliably: near the optimum the steps are then decided by the noise, and a
fit wanders until its iteration limit. With the settings of `model.R` the value is accurate to
below $10^{-6}$ and the gradient to below $10^{-4}$: the default `gtol` of $10^{-6}$ lies below the
noise of the gradient, and the default `ftol` hardly above that of the value. `model.R`
sets the tolerances of the optimiser an order of magnitude above the noise; the fits and profiles
of the following chapters use them.

```{r tolerances}
```

Tighter tolerances of the solver allow tighter tolerances of the optimiser, at a higher cost of
every evaluation.
